title: plugin-unload-kv-migration-trt-triton-exploratory-notes
content:
Objective:
Quick experimental notes exploring safe plugin unload and KV-cache migration strategies when swapping between TensorRT kernels, Triton-backed ensembles, and custom CUDA ops. Goal is to minimize end-to-end tail latency and correctness/regression risk during live kernel swaps or forced fallbacks under pressure (memory/thermal/driver errors).

Context / motivation:
- We frequently need to move inference processing between: TensorRT-optimized kernels, Triton model ensembles (which may host a smaller precision variant), and our in-house custom-kernel path (for ops TritT/Trt doesnt support).
- Live swaps happen for: degraded device health, overloaded GPU mem, scheduled rollouts, or canary experimentation.
- KV cache is large for long-context chat use-cases; migrating or preserving it across kernel boundaries is critical to avoid cost of recomputing prefixes or corrupting generation.

High-level design constraints:
- Safety: no dropped tokens or corrupted KV state. If migration cannot be done safely, degrade gracefully (stall + offload + replay) rather than risk wrong completions.
- Latency SLOs: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 120ms for short responses. Swaps should try to stay bounded (target swap p95 < 500ms).
- Memory: avoid doubling GPU memory usage during migration (i.e., avoid full simultaneous duplicate KV on GPU + host).
- Simplicity: prefer solutions that require minimal model format changes or minimal per-model kernel plumbing.

Explored strategies (notes + microbench results):
1) Copy-on-GPU then switch pointer (eager copy + atomic swap)
  - Flow: allocate destination buffers on GPU for new kernel, copy full KV from old buffers, validate checksums, atomically flip pointers, free old KV.
  - Pros: immediate post-swap performance; KV stays on GPU; no replay.
  - Cons: requires extra peak-GPU-memory = size(KV); for long contexts (eg 1.5M tokens in kv-like representation) this is infeasible. Also expensive for live systems with tight memory.
  - Microbench: KV size 2.4GB -> copy time ~420ms (cudaMemcpy async + synchronize), checksum 18ms, pointer flip ~3ms. Total observed swap p95 ~460ms (exceeded preferred for bigger KV).

2) Incremental chunked copy (streamed handover)
  - Flow: copy KV in N chunks while old kernel continues serving reads for prefixes. Mark ranges as migrated; new kernel can read migrated ranges; fallback to old for not-yet-migrated ranges. After full copy, flip to new kernel.
  - Pros: bounded extra memory (size of chunk), reduces pause time, allows serving during migration.
  - Cons: introduces cross-kernel read routing complexity (need routing layer to multiplex KV reads), potential consistency hazards if generation writes back. Also increases per-token read latency for ranges needing cross-kernel fetch.
  - Microbench: chunk size 32MB, KV total 2.4GB, copy throughput ~6GB/s -> total copy time ~400ms but no single blocking pause; per-token read overhead for cross-boundary ~1.6ms p95. End-to-end swap p95 observed ~210ms (good), but p99 tail for some sequences ~980ms due to small numbers of writes crossing chunk boundaries.

3) Offload-cache (evict-to-host and refill on-demand)
  - Flow: move KV to host (pinned CPU memory) or NVMe-persistent cache; free GPU; new kernel lazily pages-in KV ranges on demand via DMA.
  - Pros: eliminates need for duplicate GPU allocation; small peak GPU mem; safe if host has capacity.
  - Cons: severe latency impact for cold pages; requires robust prefetcher and eviction heuristics; NVMe paths impose ms-level stalls per miss.
  - Microbench: NVMe prefetch + DMA mean cold miss ~8–20ms; host-pinned CPU ~2–6ms. For interactive tail sensitive apps, cold misses unacceptable without aggressive prefetch.

4) Recompute-from-prefix (replay strategy)
  - Flow: in place of moving KV, re-run the initial prefix tokens on the new kernel to rebuild KV locally (could be done on GPU or CPU).
  - Pros: no migration plumbing; consistent KV semantics; avoids holding duplicate KV.
  - Cons: expensive CPU/GPU cycles for long prefixes; increases cost and latency proportional to prefix length. For chat with long histories, unacceptable.
  - Microbench: 1200 tokens replay on GPU with quantized kernels ~150ms; on CPU ~2.1s.

5) Hybrid pointer + small replays (sparse patching)
  - Flow: copy/transfer head-of-history KV ranges (recent context) eagerly; patch older KV regions lazily by replaying only anchor checkpoints (every K tokens). Combining chunked copy for head + replay for older parts reduces memory and latency costs.
  - Pros: good latency for the common case (recent tokens matter more); reduces peak memory compared to full copy.
  - Cons: complexity and bookkeeping for checkpoints; slightly higher implementation cost.
  - Microbench: eager head 128KB buckets for last 1024 tokens -> copy ~22ms; older region patches replayed in background; swap p95 ~180ms.

6) Zero-copy cross-kernel access shim (unified memory view)
  - Flow: abstract the KV as a logical object with backend adapters. If both kernels can honor same memory layout, we map physical memory and avoid copying.
  - Pros: near zero migration cost.
  - Cons: requires strict ABI compatibility between kernels (TensorRT vs custom op layouts differ), or adapter glue that translates on-the-fly (which is expensive). Requires changes to kernel build processes.

Observations re: Triton + TRT + custom kernels:
- TensorRT serialized engines pack tensors differently (optimized for perf) vs our custom kernel library which expects packed KV of different stride/pinned-locs. Converting layout on the fly costs non-trivial time.
- Triton provides nice model-level lifecycle hooks (load/unload), but kernel-level pointer swap isn't a first-class primitive for multi-plugin models. We end up doing model-level handoffs that implicate larger memory scopes than needed.
- When Triton manages both the TRTEngine and a custom plugin, the path of least resistance was to perform chunked in-GPU copy orchestrated by a lightweight controller running in the runtime process instead of asking Triton to do cross-model copies. This keeps orchestration logic in our runtime.

Failure modes and safety margins:
- In-flight writes: generation may write to KV while migration occurs; must use compare-and-swap epoch markers for each token write. Migration must capture a consistent epoch snapshot or stall writers until the chunk is in a consistent state.
- Driver-level failures: fallback must guarantee that a previously-accepted request still completes on fallback kernel or is retried—avoid silent drop.

Suggested fallback policy (pragmatic):
- Trigger conditions: sudden memory pressure, kernel TDR, retriable Triton model load errors, scheduled canary cutover.
- Primary strategy: chunked-copy Head+Lazy-Patch (strategy 5). Reason: balances memory and latency with limited implementation complexity.
- If GPU peak memory required for head+chunking > 60% of available, fall back to offload-to-host with aggressive prefetcher and a per-request soft-timeout that will replay if fetch takes too long.
- For critical low-latency customers, disable live kernel swaps—require reserved capacity or prefer Canary rolling across replicas.

Instrumentation and metrics to add (experimentally valuable):
- Per-swap timeline events: start_copy, chunk_complete, checksum_ok, pointer_flip, free_old. Emit trace ids per request to correlate token-level latency with migration events.
- KV read percentiles split by location (local kernel buffer vs remote kernel read vs host vs NVMe).
- Migration-related error counters and retry rates.

Implementation notes / TODOs:
- Build a small migration controller lib (C++) that exposes: begin_migration(snapshot_epoch), read_chunk(offset,length), finalize_migration(), abort_migration(). Keep it kernel-agnostic and pluggable.
- Add per-range epoch markers in KV writes, with light-weight fencing (atomic counters). Minimal change to generation loop: increment epoch per write batch.
- Prototype chunked-copy controller as userspace process using CUDA IPC for peer copies to avoid host round-trips. Test on multi-GPU NVLink vs PCIe to understand throughput differences.

Prototype results summary (quick):
- Chunked Head+Lazy patch wins for medium contexts: swap p95 ~170–210ms, p99 ~420ms; extra peak mem ~chunk_size (configurable 32–128MB).
- Full eager copy only feasible for small KV (<500MB); otherwise memory cost too high.
- Offload-to-host okay for non-interactive batch workloads; not for low-latency interactive chat without very aggressive prefetching and huge host bandwidth.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- GPU peercopy vs staged host pinned copies: measure for NVLink-enabled machines; is total latency dominated by memcpy or kernel scheduling jitter?
- Interaction with quantized TRT engines: does converting layout + float16->int8 mapping add a deterministic conversion step that we can accelerate with custom kernels?
- Can we extend Triton plugin API to request a buffer-migrate RPC instead of reloading models? Feasibility study with Triton maintainers.
- Evaluate cost model: when is it cheaper to accept a small replay vs maintaining duplicate KV on GPU in terms of $/request.

Appendix: quick checklist for safe rollout
- [ ] Add migration controller integration tests (unit + e2e with synthetic KV sizes)
- [ ] Add epoch fencing and verify no-write windows are bounded and logged
- [ ] Add metrics and tracing for swap timeline
- [ ] Add feature flag to pick migration strategy per-customer workload profile
- [ ] Run canary across ~10 pods with long-chat workload; observe p95/p99; prove no loss of token sequence continuity

Notes to self: these are largely exploratory; prefer small incremental PRs: (1) epoch markers + controller interface, (2) chunked-copy implementation w/ NVLink test, (3) telemetry + failure-mode tests.

End of notes.
